utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Just for full transparency, yesterday I'd forgotten to instruct the witness not to speak with anyone. I noticed that immediately after I left the courtroom. I took care that this message was conveyed to the witness through the Victims and Witnesses Section. Mr. Radosevic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Emmerson, are you ready to continue the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if it's of any assistance to Your Honours, I understand that counsel for the other accused will not be cross-examining in terms of time. Could we put up the map P10, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And whilst that's being done, may I ask you one or two questions arising from the matters that were being discussed yesterday afternoon. You were telling us yesterday afternoon, Mr. Radosevic, that after you left your father's house, you stopped off at the Stijovic house in Bandera to try to pick up Novak's father's rifle but that there was no one at the home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You also told us earlier in your testimony that it was at the -- at Bandera that you were stopped by Caus and two other men with guns; is that right as well?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And yesterday you told us that -- in the afternoon, you told us that Caus stopped you at the crossroads in Bandera leading to Gornji and Donji Ratis on one side and Ljubarda on the other side. Again, is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we just please zoom in on the area which shows Dashinoc, Bandera, Pozhare. Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, can you just locate yourself. You can see Dashinoc, you can see Bandera and you can see Pozhare. You told us that you took the southern road from Dashinoc to Pozhare via Bandera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about north and south, but that's the one road that I always used.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There were two ways you could go from Dashinoc, are there not? You could go north, straight to the road that runs from Decani to Maznik, or you could go on the south road via Bandera to Pozhare; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, why would I go round about? I could have also gone via Klina. What I took was a shorter road from Dasinovac to Decani. I don't see why I would go --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radosevic, if you would just listen to what I'm asking you. I'm not asking you why you took it, and I'm not questioning your reasoning for taking it, I'm simply asking you to confirm that you did. And that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Dasinovac, Bandera, and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right. Can you, taking the pen, please, can you mark for us where on the road from Dashinoc to Bandera the Stijovic house is, please.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately here. I'm not quite certain, but this is roughly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just to orientate ourselves, I think we can see just a little to the left of that the crossroads that you're referring to at Bandera, where the road goes north towards Ljubarda and south towards Gornji and Donji Ratis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, before we continue, I missed the moment when the witness marked. Is that just above the letter A in Bandera? Perhaps you could enlarge it a tiny little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see a red dot on there, but it's hardly --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we zoom a little bit on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Don't mark it again. Let's just zoom in on the picture; we can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or perhaps add a letter of the family name to that so that we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you put the letter S against your dot, please, the letter S?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And just to the left of that, I think you were about to confirm, is the crossroads that you're referring to where you were intercepted by Caus; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radosevic, I'm not asking you to give an explanation at the moment, but we have a signed statement from you made to the Prosecution on the 26th of January, 2002. I'm just asking you to confirm - we will have the document - you didn't, in fact, mention stopping at the Stijovic house in that statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention because I had no reason to mention, because I didn't find his rifle. If I had found his rifle there in his house, I would have mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: After you had been to the Stijovic house and failed to find a weapon, you therefore still had only one gun; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think you confirmed yesterday that when Caus and the other men stopped you, you told him that you were going to Decane to get the other gun, and you said the same thing a little later on to the men at the crossroads in Pozhare. You told them that you were going to Decane to get the other gun. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But, in fact, as you told us yesterday, you never had any intention of going to Decane to get the gun; you were just lying to them to get through their checkpoints. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to save my skin. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that. But the point I'm asking you to be clear about is that you were lying to them, and you had no intention of going to Decane to get a gun. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was Novak living in Decane at that time, or did he have a flat or a premises there?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a flat in which they lived from time to time. When they worked late, they would stay there overnight, but most of the time they did not live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you say "they," do you mean the whole family or do you mean Novak and his brothers?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novak and brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they worked up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to believe that they would have a gun in their flat in Decane?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What are you getting at?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Don't worry about what I'm getting at. Please just answer the question. If you don't understand it, I'll repeat it. Did you have any reason at that time to believe that Novak or his brothers themselves had a gun in their flat in Decane?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether their gun was at Decani or at Bandera. My purpose was to save my skin, to lie successfully to that group of people, to save my life. Whether his gun was at Bandera or elsewhere, whether they believed me or not, that was not the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Radosevic, I just want to ask you one question, if I may, about an interview that you gave to Mr. Dutertre when you arrived in The Hague on Monday of this week. Do you remember that he showed you those NGO documents that you've been asked to comment on in your evidence, when you first arrived here?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you first arrived in The Hague on Monday, you had a meeting with Mr. Dutertre, the gentleman sitting -- if you just look over on the other side of the court; yes?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And during that meeting, he showed you some NGO documents, the ones that you were shown during your evidence, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he asked you to then comment on them or correct them, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we see, please, the notes from that proofing session, which I think are only available in hard copy, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- Madam Registrar has a copy for the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps first we'll give a number to the new marked map.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you in need of any further markings that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think not for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because, of course, we are trying to avoid that we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Multiple markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not multiple markings on one map but we have 15 maps on the same event.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps it should stay up for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll leave it for the moment. And I take it, Madam Registrar, that that's possible, to have the proofing notes on the ELMO and at the same time leave the map on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think we simply have to switch channels on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, these are not translated into Serbian, and so it's the second page, please, rather than the first that we need to put up. If you can just put the second sheet up.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to look at the second line. I'm not asking you to read that, Mr. Radosevic, because obviously you won't be able to read it because it is only recorded in English. But at this point, you were being asked about the "Spotlight" report and to correct what was said there. And you are recorded as having said, and I'll read it slowly so it can be translated: "I went with a rifle that belonged to my late father. And then I went to Decane to get Novak's rifle that actually belonged to Novak's father." I just want to understand this, Mr. Radosevic: Were you going to Decane to get Novak's rifle or not? Because you seem to have told Mr. Dutertre that you were; whereas you told the Tribunal that you had no such intention?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm telling you once again: I stopped by that house, and if I had found that rifle, I would have maybe gone to Glodjane. Since I didn't find it, I went to Decani. I had said to them that I would go and get that rifle, but practically I was lying to them to save my skin, because from Pozare to Decani, a thousand different thoughts went through my head. What will happen if I bring the second rifle as well? Maybe then they wouldn't let me go either. I lied that I would go to Decani and get it, and in the end we all remained alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It may not be a massive point, Mr. Radosevic. I'm simply trying to ascertain this: If Mr. Dutertre correctly recorded what you were trying to say to him, you seem to have been suggesting that you were going to get a rifle that you believed to be in Decane, whereas in fact, as I understand it, that's not right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I told that gentleman that I was going to Decani to that other rifle, but it was a lie that I told them. I was trying to protect myself, to get out of that situation and to get my mother out and my friend out. What if I had gotten that rifle in Decani and returned to Glodjane? Maybe I wouldn't have returned alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on, if we may. I asked you some questions yesterday about whether these men who assaulted you on the road from Irzniq to Gllogjan when the car broke down, whether they were asking you questions about the police operation on the 24th of March, asking for information about the police, and so forth, or whether you were just being ill-treated because of your ethnicity. And I want to ask you this: You've told us that your mother was not ill-treated, and I want to put to you one passage in the signed statement that you made to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, I don't ask it be brought up, but for the note, it's page 6, the sixth full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm just going to read to you, again slowly for translation, what is recorded there. You said this: "I said that they could do what they wished with me but to leave my mother alone. The man with the sniper rifle asked me, 'Is this your mother?' When I replied in the affirmative, he said, 'Then she is my mother, too,' and he told the other soldiers not to harm her?" Do you remember the man saying to you that if she was your mother, then she was his mother, too?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He said that. I told him that he could do whatever he wanted to me but to leave alone my mother. She was an elderly woman. But I don't see why they wouldn't give her a glass of water to take her pill. Later we were taken into that house. She remained outside. But it's true that that man said that they should leave her alone from that time on, that they shouldn't interrogate her, because they had already started to curse her because she didn't know the Albanian language. I said, Right, she doesn't speak Albanian, don't question her, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I then move to the time that you spent with your father that day. Again, just for clarity, you told us that he had two guns in the house and that you took one of the two guns away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, presumably, the reason you only took one gun was you didn't want to leave your father completely unarmed?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. He asked me for one rifle and that's why I took one rifle. Why would I give him two rifles? Why would I have to give somebody a rifle just like that? I can't see a reason to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What was the gun that you left your father with?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your father was 55, I think; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He knew how to use the rifle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did. He was a -- he used to hunt. He didn't buy this rifle for decoration purposes. He bought it to go hunting, so he knew how to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can I just ask you briefly about the clothes that he was wearing when you saw him. I think you told the Prosecution in a signed statement that when you went to identify your father's clothing, you particularly recognised a camouflage jacket that he'd been wearing on the day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that the following morning, that is, after this incident, you spoke to a friend of yours called Slavisa Markovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I'm going to ask the witness some questions arising out of his testimony yesterday. And I wonder if it would be helpful using the -- obviously, I was working overnight from the transcript provided at the end of the day, so I've provided to Your Honours copies of the transcript, so that Your Honours can follow the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have all the transcripts on our screen in e-court so we can switch from one transcript to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you to follow it on the paper copy is because the pagination which I was using from last night will not necessarily correspond with the pagination that currently appears on e-court. Obviously, we can cross-refer in due course if there are any differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you refer to specific wording, you can immediately find it, and this would save, however, would to avoid --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll follow that practice, if I may, in future. But I'm looking at the moment at page 12 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that the following morning, Mr. Markovic told you that at about 7.00 to 7.30 in the evening the night before, he had heard a lot of gun-fire which he thought must have been the attack on your father's house, and you told us that he could hear this from a kilometre and a half away. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, he told you that there was a lot of gun-fire. Did he tell you how long this gun-fire went on for?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to make it clear: I'm not challenging that there was gun-fire. A number of witnesses, I think, heard an exchange of fire coming from the direction of your father's house that night. But I want to come, if I can now, to the conversation that you say you had with your Albanian neighbour, that is, the man that you're not willing to name. Now, that conversation took place on the same day that you went to the scene where your father's body had been found; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the next day when I went to look where my father had been found, I turned around and I met this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When you went there to the scene, were there police officers around at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the next day when I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And was that the only occasion that you went there?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there once again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So this was the first occasion that you went there?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time that I went there. After having found my father, I went there the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's be clear. When was the first time you went to the place that your father's body had been found? I'm not asking for the date, but was it after your father's body had been removed?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And on that first occasion, do I understand you correctly, there were no police officers there when you got there?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no need for them to be there because -- so there was -- there were no police there when I went to see the place where my father had been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just please, if you will, just confine yourself to answering the question for the moment. You say you went there again after that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice or three times. I can't remember, but I passed by two or three times. Two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were there police officers there on any of those occasions?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we please look at Defence document identification 1507. I think this is already exhibited as D5. Oh, I'm sorry, could we save the map? I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you don't need the map anymore. Then, Madam Registrar -- if, yes, if we have to show D5, then this one should be, yes, stored. Okay. Madam Registrar, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number D6, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is there any objection against admission? There's not, so it can be admitted right away. D6 is admitted. Then the next one to be on the screen is D5, as far as I understand? I think we should use the words "Exhibit D5" for purposes of linking it to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exhibit D5, yes. Could we look, please, to page 4 of that document, and paragraph 18. And can we enlarge paragraph 18, please, and 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm just going to read to you, again slowly, what you said or are recorded as having said in a statement that you signed on the 23rd of August of 2005 last year. You said this: "I was present when the bodies of Slobodan Radosevic and Milos Radunovic were located by police in September 1998. I was with Zoran Nikic, my cousin, and Novak Vlahovic, my neighbour. Somebody had thrown earth over their bodies, but they had not been buried in a grave, they just lay on the ground with earth covering them. I can't recall the names of the 15 to 20 police officers securing and investigating at the scene, but I will be able to find out their names when I return to work." And then you say: "When I arrived at the scene, the bodies had been removed and placed into body bags?" Now, were there 15 to 20 police officers securing the scene when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, so this is paragraph 18, some things are not quite clear here. I told Mr. Kelly, I think that's his name, that I was with Novak Vlahovic when Zoran Radunovic told me that the remains of Milos Radunovic and Slobodan Radosevic had been found, and he told me that I couldn't go to Dasinovac, telling me that there were 15 to 20 police officers doing the on-site investigation and so on, and that I couldn't go to the village of Dasinovac on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you were told, were you, by Mr. Nikic that there were 15 to 20 police officers there?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, conducting an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Now, the records that we have state that your father's remains were removed on the 10th of September, so that would --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We can remove this from the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- so that would place your first visit there when you say you spoke to your Albanian neighbour as being the 11th of September; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 9th that my father was found, but the 10th -- well, I'm not very sure about the dates, but what I do know is that I went there the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. The date I was putting to you was the date on which his remains were removed from the scene, and the records suggest that his remains were removed on the 10th. Now, you're telling us you went the following day, so that would put your first visit at the 11th, wouldn't it, if those records are right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the dates. So my father was found on one day, and then the next day I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to clarify with you, please, if we can, a number of points about what you say this Albanian neighbour of yours told you?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And for Your Honours' reference, I'm looking at transcript page 26, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Mr. Radosevic, I think you told us yesterday that this man told you that he had not seen your father and Mr. Radunovic being captured; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is true that he was not there when they were captured, but after that, when they passed by his house, he stopped the cars and he saw them in the cars. He couldn't see whether they had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Pause there. Pause there. So he told you he couldn't see whether they had been wounded, did he?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us that he told you that they were headed from Dashinoc towards the Pozhare crossroads; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were moving from Dasinovac in the direction of Decani. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is transcript page 29, line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- you told us yesterday that you assumed that they must have been heading for Gllogjan because that is where you and others had been taken; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right that I'd said that. They would not have taken them to Decani. They took all of the captives to their headquarters in Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about what you assumed. This is not something that the witness you're describing, this Albanian man, told you, is it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are my assumptions, that they wanted to take them to Glodjane. But he told me that they were actually heading to Pozare. But it wasn't quite clear to me. It was the same situation as it was with me. They had no need to take me to Pozare; they took me to Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And Pozhare is a crossroads that goes in a number of different directions; is that right? A simple yes or no will do, Mr. Radosevic.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether these men were wearing uniforms or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think as far as I remember, but I'm not sure, I seem to recall that they were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You seem to recall. Did he tell it to you or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether, like Mr. Markovic, he had heard the sound of a lot of gun-fire coming from your father's house and from that direction?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that there had been shooting in the area around my house, and in the morning the people that were taking him to Ratis, they told him about my father, that he had been captured, and that his fate was unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pause. You're confusing the two incidents. It may be my fault. The question I'm asking you is not about what Mr. Markovic told you but whether your Albanian friend that you say you spoke to, whether he confirmed that there had been a lot of gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I really can't remember whether he told me that he had heard shooting or not, so I don't want to tell you something that I'm not certain of.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Surely, Mr. Radosevic, that's the first question you would have asked him, is it not? Did you hear gun-fire, if you wanted -- if you're really talking to somebody who had seen your father in a car and who couldn't tell you whether he was injured or not, and you tell us you had already heard that there had been gun-fire. Surely the first question you would have asked him is, Did you hear an exchange of fire around my father's house?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, maybe that was an omission on my part that I failed to ask him whether there had been any shooting around my house, but at that time I really didn't care whether he was injured or killed in my house, in Glodjane, in Prilep, in Maznik, because the only thing I wanted at that time was to find out -- to find out who it was. But he wasn't able to tell me who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For all you knew, your father may have been shot in an exchange of fire and injured in the back of those cars while he was being driven away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not disputing that. You told us one of the rumours you'd heard of was that he might have died from gun-shot injuries and bled to death. I'm simply asking you whether you were not concerned to find out from this man if there had been a fire-fight?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that yesterday, the rumours that I heard, but then His Honour interrupted me. I heard rumours that he had been brought to the village of Prilep, together with Milos Radunovic, that they were wounded, and the rumour had it that Milos had been wounded in the hand. And they took them to the village of Prilep, but the people from the village of Prilep didn't want to let them stay there because they were afraid that then they would be blamed for it. So they went from Prilep to Glodjane, and the rumour had it that they died there or in the village of Dasinovac. But these were just rumours that I heard, that I picked up. I wanted to share that with you yesterday, but then the Judges interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, you did share it with us yesterday. It's on the transcript, Mr. Radosevic. The point is, one of the rumours that you heard was that they may have bled to death from injuries sustained to their hands and legs in a fire-fight, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he was wounded in Dasinovac, Glodjane, Prilep, Bandera. I can't tell you because I did not witness that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you don't know whether he fired first on these people or they fired first, do you, from anything that you've seen yourself or been told?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we just look, please, for Your Honours, at transcript page 26, line 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Radosevic, you were asked these questions by Mr. Dutertre. He asked you: "When he," that is, the Albanian man, "stopped them, did he tell you what means of transportation they were using, Milos Radunovic and Slobodan your father?" And you replied: "Well, he said that it was by car, but he didn't specify the make. And he said the persons, the soldiers, were not from the village of Dasinovac." And then Mr. Dutertre asked you: "How many cars were they? Did he tell you?" And you replied: "No, he didn't." Your evidence was, when asked this question by Mr. Dutertre first, that this man didn't tell you how many cars there were. Do you understand what I'm putting to you? Yes? And then a little later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 29, line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Dutertre asked you this: "Let me go back a little. How many soldiers were they when he stopped them to try and save your father as well as Milos Radunovic?" And you replied: "Well, from what he told me, they were in two cars, so maybe seven or eight of them." Now, that's your evidence yesterday, Mr. Radosevic. Just to be clear, when you were first asked, you said that this man did not tell you how many cars there were, and then when asked to say how many people there were, you said he told you there were two cars. Now, are you making this account of what this man told you up as you're going along?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. If my memory serves me right, I said that there were two cars, and I didn't know what make they were. I don't know how -- I think that if I remember correctly, I said that I didn't know exactly how many cars but that there may have been two, maybe seven or eight people in them. I think that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was your second answer, Mr. Radosevic. Your first answer categorically was that he did not tell you how many cars there were. And I'm asking you whether you're making this up as you're going along?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not making this up. But I think that the first question was the make of the car, and then I said that this man didn't know what make those cars were, but that there were two cars and maybe seven or eight people, and that it was, in fact, correct that these people were not from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you also told us --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And this is, Your Honours, pages 26, lines 6 to 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- you said this: "When he had been captured, when they headed from my house towards Glodjane, he stopped there. He stood in the road, maybe 5 or 6 metres down the road, and he just stopped them." Did this man tell you that he'd stopped them 5 or 6 metres down the road? Was he as specific as that, or is this something that you yourself have invented?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think that there may be a misunderstanding. I said 500 to 600 metres away from the house, so maybe it was a problem with the interpretation or transcript. I said 500 or 600 metres away from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he tell you 500 or 600 metres, or is that something you've made up?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me where he stopped them, 5 or 600 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So he gave you that specific information, but you didn't ask him whether there'd been an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I had not asked him about whether there had been a fire-fight or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radosevic, have you had an opportunity to look at the witness statement you made to the Prosecution in this case?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You never told the Prosecution, did you, that there was a man who'd seen your father being driven away, even if you weren't willing to name him. You never told the Prosecution before you came into court that there was a man who'd actually seen them on the night, did you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not the night, it was day-time. But I didn't want to introduce this person at all because I was afraid that somebody might harm him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You never needed to give his name. You could have told the Prosecution that there was someone whose name you couldn't give who'd actually seen your father being driven away. You didn't tell the Prosecution that at any time before you came into court, did you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Radosevic, you mentioned a man called Deli Lekaj. You were asked by Mr. Dutertre about a man called Deli Lekaj who you'd heard had been involved in the incident. I want to put something to you. Did you know that Deli Lekaj had been shot by your father in the leg that night and taken to hospital?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You've never heard that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Do you know Rade Vlahovic? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he never told you that, your friend?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Are you telling us the truth, Mr. Radosevic, about this? I'm going to give you another opportunity. Did your friend or any of your friends ever tell you that the man you'd given evidence about, Deli Lekaj, was shot in the leg by your father in a fire-fight at Dashinoc? You seem to have heard quite a lot of rumours.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm hearing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Let's go back just for a moment, can we, please, to the scene when you went to visit the area where your father's body had been found. You told us you were in that area on three or four occasions, is that right, in total?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three times. Let's say three. I'm not sure. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Two or three times after the occasion when you first went, or two or three times in all?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What were you doing there on those other occasions?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the second time I was there, I wanted to light a candle at the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Radosevic, forgive me, because you may or may not know this, but there was an international presence in the area around that time. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second time I went?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: At around this period of time, there were international monitors in the area. Did you know that; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went there, I didn't see anyone. I wasn't aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radosevic, a large number of the Albanian houses in Dashinoc and the surrounding villages had been looted by the police and burnt by the time you say you first went there. Did you see the evidence of the houses of your Albanian neighbours, people you've told us were your friends, had been burnt down? Did you see that or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them, the same as mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And do you know who burnt them down?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You've got a lot of friends in the police, haven't you? You've told us yesterday that you recognise a lot of people in the police. You really don't know who burnt down all the houses of the Albanians in Dashinoc in September?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure you can infer from this, Mr. Radosevic, it wasn't the Albanians who burnt their own houses down, was it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You do know, I suggest, Mr. Radosevic. You know that these houses were looted and burned by paramilitary police along with a group of young Serbs from the area in revenge, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me give you the names of the houses that were burnt down and see if you recognise your neighbours. Halil Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Shaban and Avdullah Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Qaush Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that name. I know the last name but not the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Muharrem Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sadri Kadrijaj?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Ghafer Kadrijaj?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard that name. I know the family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Asmon Gradinaj?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Dede Gjokaj. Dede Gjokaj?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about him. I mean I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I've just read you a long list of names that covers rather a large number of your neighbours, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We lived together in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for the name of the person you say you spoke to on the day that you attended, but can you tell us -- are you willing to tell us whether his name was one of the names I've just read out to you on that long list; yes or no? And you can do it in private session if you wish, just whether his name is on that long list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson gives you an opportunity to ask for a private session if you'd prefer to answer his question in private session; that is, that no one will hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to say anything about that man who tried to save my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you this, Mr. Radosevic: Was that man's house burnt down as well?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably, just like mine and the other Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I ask you again: What were you doing on these three or four occasions when you were in that area after the Serb forces had taken control?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited the place where my father's body was found, I visited my home and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know Ahmet Sokolaj, or did you know Ahmet Sokolaj?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think his real name is Ahmed. His name is Ahmet, and he was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He was the house very near to yours, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about an incident that happened involving him, because you've told us how close your relationships were with your friendly neighbours. On the 3rd of April, 1999, a group of Albanians was stopped trying to leave the area by police officers and paramilitaries next to the police station in Decani, and Ahmet Sokolaj, the elderly father, was taken out and beaten and subsequently killed. Mr. Radosevic, I suggest you were there when that happened?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. I heard about it from Vela Petar when I went to the village and talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From his son Aki, from my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There were a lot of people there on that day, Mr. Radosevic. You're sure you weren't there, outside the police station in Decane?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I've just one or two further matters, if I may. The area where you -- which was pointed out to you as the area where your father's remains had been found, is it possible to describe that as Bandera?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because the records record that your father's body was found in Bandera.

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I lived there for 23 years, that place was never called Bandera. It's on the tripartite boundary between Vodolija [phoen], Ratis and Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you know that your father's remains had been removed from that place and taken to the Lake Radonjic canal before they were taken to Hotel Pastrik? Was that something that you were told or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So this is the first time that you're being informed of that fact, is it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, they were, and they were then taken to Hotel Pastrik. Now, I just want to ask you a little bit about the process that followed on from that, because I need some clarification about what it was exactly that was shown to you and when. Could we look, please, at your statement of the 23rd of August again, which I think is D5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, before you continue, I see on page 28, line 10, you tell us what happened. That's quite extraordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, if it's not a matter in dispute, it's as between parties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not aware of -- I have not seen any agreed fact that this has happened. So is that confirm, Mr. Dutertre? That's not a matter in dispute, that the body of the witness's father was first taken to the Lake Radonjic canal before they were taken to Hotel Pastrik. Is that not in dispute? Mr. Emmerson is giving us a fact, and Mr. Emmerson is supposed not to give evidence. Therefore, I wonder what -- for what reason he tells us, and he now tells us that this is, more or less, an agreed fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it's not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this comes out of the evidence which the Prosecution has received. The Prosecution does not deny that the bodies were first taken to the lake, where they were then given to the medical -- at the canal, yes, at the canal, for provisional keeping. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps I should have made that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't clear to me at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So we have a statement -- your statement of the 23rd of August, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at paragraphs 19 and 20. In the English as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Radosevic, in paragraphs 19 and 20, I just want to be clear, you say that the day after you arrived at the scene you went to Hotel Pastrik, and there you saw the skeleton remains of your father, and you saw various other items of his clothing and artefacts as well. And then at paragraph 20, you say this: "When I identified my father's remains ... there was not a full skeleton there, and I recall seeing the bones separate from the clothing. It is possible that the bones located belonging to both Slobodan Radosevic and Milos Radunovic could be mixed up. I don't think that the bones were examined too thoroughly?" Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in English. I really don't know English.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do apologise. You should have the Serbian translation in front of you. Oh, I'm sorry, it's an Albanian translation. You don't read Albanian. Do you read Albanian, Mr. Radosevic?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I speak Albanian, but I really -- but not really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Radosevic, in that case let me just read it out to you again, and I'll summarise, I hope, fairly. You say in the statement made in August of last year that when you went to the hotel, you saw the skeleton remains of your father as well as other things belonging to him. You say that it was not a full skeleton, and that you recalled seeing the bones separate from the clothing. You then say: "It is possible that the bones of Slobodan Radosevic and Milos Radunovic could have been mixed up" because you didn't think they had been examined too thoroughly. So that's the first passage I want to take you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I'm happy for that to be marked for identification, but I'm not asking at the moment for it to be -- oh, it is already an exhibit, that one. I'm sorry. The second passage doesn't need to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, that we now look at a statement you made four months later in December, slightly less than four months later in December 2005. This is Defence document identification 1522.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has no number yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It has no exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want to tender that or do you just want to read from it?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm just happy to read from it. So we can mark it for identification, but I shan't, for the moment, be asking for it to be tendered, unless anybody else wants it to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number D7, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, again, I'll just read this to you slowly. You say here -- so we're now at paragraph 7 of this statement, please, which is on page 2. In --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it hasn't come up yet, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You say this: "In September I went to Hotel Pastrik to identify the remains of my father Slobodan Radosevic. I was there with my brother Radoje Radosevic, and we identified my father's clothing. My father's remains were in a black plastic bag, and I was not allowed to view the remains," -- "I was not allowed to review the remains because the Serbian investigative team did not want us to see the remains as they believed it was better to remember our relatives the way they were when they were alive. I assumed that the body was incomplete because the body was open to the elements for a long time." You then say: "It's usual to put clothes into a coffin." And you say: "After we identified the clothing, we were told that we would have to wait for the identification procedure to be completed as there was co-mingling of the bones between Milos Radunovic and Slobodan Radosevic, and it would take longer than normal." So you left and you say: "I didn't see the remains of my father either being put into the coffin or being in the coffin at any stage." And then you say: "On the 18th of September, we received the wooden coffin." Now, I just want to ask you, first of all: In the first of those two statements, you say that you did see the remains, the bones of your father; and in the second, you say that you did not? Now, I don't want to take a great deal of time on this and I don't want an explanation for the discrepancy. I'm just asking you: Did you or did you not see the bones, or were bones pointed out to you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to explain this. They did not allow me to reveal the remains. I saw a part of the bones. There must be a mistake, just like in the previous instance with 5 and 6 metres, and 5 and 600 metres. I saw some of the bones and I saw the belongings. It is true that it is a custom in our parts to dress the dead body and to follow a certain procedure, but they said that in this case it was not really possible because the remains were highly decomposed. And it's true that Milos Radunovic and Slobodan Radosevic were found together and the bones, I'm sure, did get mixed up. It is true that I took over that coffin which had a tin casket inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And, again, I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: My brother actually took that coffin.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. Radosevic, I'm at this stage simply seeking to establish the reality of what was given to you, and I think when the coffin finally came, it was sealed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tin one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And there had been a delay because of the -- as you had been told, there had been a delay because of co-mingling?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, again, I'm going to put something to the witness which is not in dispute between the parties, so that Your Honour is aware. If there's any objection when I put it, Mr. Dutertre will correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radosevic, there's evidence in this case that your father's bones were co-mingled not only with bones of Milos Radunovic but that there was co-mingling with bones of individuals found at the canal. Was that explained to you or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Dutertre frowning. It may be that this an issue we need to discuss between ourselves. But what is clear on the record is that the witness was not told that, if it is, in fact, the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and there's no evidence for that. At least the witness did not tell us that he heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's the important point. That's the important point. It wasn't communicated to the witness. As to whether it's right or not, if Mr. Dutertre is not familiar with the material, then we can discuss it at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the issue of whether it's in dispute, we'll hear from you at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. On the one hand, I don't really quite see what we are getting at, because I think we have agreed on identification by genetic analysis on the first bodies, D-1 and D-2, Slobodan Radosevic and -- the two bodies at any rate. And, in addition, I think we are discussing matters which the following witnesses will discuss. But this does leave an opportunity to the Defence counsel to discuss it. We have discovered human remains which were attributed to those two people that have been compared with the other remains found in the lake. These are things which might be mentioned by following witnesses. These remains have been put in a bag, and together with other bags -- found in other bags, all found. At any rate, I don't think that we can talk about a mixing up or co-mingled, but some bones could not be attributed to the bodies. Some of the remains have been buried in Piskote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait and hear on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The only question I needed to know from this witness was whether -- his statement indicates that he had been informed that there was co-mingling. I simply wanted to establish whether he had been informed of co-mingling as between the two or co-mingling which included those at the lake. But we'll hear other evidence about what the actual position was in due course. So insofar as my question involved a suggestion, then there is no, as yet, evidence to substantiate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Emmerson, usually I'm late in asking what a convenient moment would be. If somewhere in the next five minutes you find a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: One more topic only.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Radosevic, I think in 2005 when Mr. Kelly came to see you, he told you that when he had gone to visit your father's grave, the bones of your father had been found still inside the black plastic body-bag but outside of the coffin, and that the grave had been opened. Do you recall him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I was an eye-witness. The grave was open, the tombstone was broken, and even the tin casket was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we just briefly look at paragraphs 12 and 13 of this same statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 12, you're commenting on this. You say you don't know why the bones were outside; you could only think that perhaps someone broke in, looking for something, and removed the bones. And then you go on at paragraph 13: "I can only think that a possible explanation for the bones being found "the way you stated" is that perhaps it was because we requested the Serbian investigation team to speed up the repatriation process and maybe they only gave us the coffin with the clothes and left the bones until later. It's only a suggestion, but perhaps the team put the bones there sometime later. This is only a theory. I have no proof whatsoever that this is the case." Did you ever make inquiries about whether the Serbian forensic team had broken into your father's grave and put the bones in afterwards, or not? Did you ever find out any further information about that?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't discuss that at all, but I know for sure that on the 14th of June, when I was withdrawing from Kosovo, around 3.00 or 4.00 p.m., I stopped by the grave of my father, and nothing had been touched. And after that, every week I visited the grave. Nothing had been dug around it. I would have seen if somebody had done any digging. But in 2005 when I went, the tombstone was vandalised, the grave was opened, the soil had been dug out, the plates had been removed, the wooden coffin was broken, and the tin one was opened. But from the day when I buried my father until the day I left Kosovo, it was intact. And in the first period we went to the grave every day, and later on we went every week, once a week. We would have noticed had anything been touched.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are the only questions I have for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do understand that other counsel -- there's no need to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There is no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Once again, we have cooperated with each other to ensure that there wouldn't be any duplication, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Mr. Dutertre, we'll have a break. Would you have any further questions to the witness? I see you're nodding yes. That's now on the record. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we'll ask the witness in again, the Chamber would like to give an oral decision on the Prosecution's notification of clarification of paragraph 89 of the indictment and request for leave to add a clarification to its pre-trial brief, filed on the 2nd of March, 2007. Paragraph 89 of the indictment reads: "Approximately," and I'm quoting, "approximately ten other people were killed while in KLA custody, and their bodies disposed of in the same location and in a similar manner to the victims identified and described above. They remain unidentified." In its notification, the Prosecution seeks to inform the Chamber that, I quote again, "evidence will be called in respect of eight unidentified victims, and not ten." The Prosecution seeks further to clarify its pre-trial brief through annex 1 of its notification. This annex is a further clarification to the allegations made in paragraph 89 of the indictment. The Defence did not object to this notification. Considering that there is no objection to the Prosecution motion by any of the Defence teams, and that in the words of the Prosecution, the motion, and I quote again, "is, in effect, a slight reduction of the allegations against the accused," the Chamber decides that annex 1 of the notification is to be added to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. This concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter. As far as UNMIK disclosure is concerned, Mr. Re, if you would have anything more to say than it's still ongoing and that everyone is still working hard on it, you're invited to do so. If that would be the message, however, then you're reminded that the Chamber would very much like to receive more concrete information soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking to the Director of Justice -- Director of the Department Of Justice later today and see if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So everyone is still doing its utmost best.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Regarding UNMIK, I had a conversation with a representative of UNMIK and understand, I believe, precisely what needs to be done, and the real question, I think at this point, is whether or not there have been requests for assistance which have been specifically made, which is what I discussed at the Pre-Trial Conference and I'll leave it at that at this time. But I believe the March 4th transcript adequately covers the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, at this moment, it's rather a reminder than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There is one other matter that did cause me some concern. I do not know whether or not there are any UNMIK files that are going to exist with regard to the two witnesses who have just been called that we were going to seek. Part of my concern in that regard is these are witnesses who were not contemplated at the time the matter was first raised on March 1st, we have no way of knowing. I don't know whether a request for assistance has been made with regard to these two particular witnesses who are coming up, 4 and 19. And in the event something comes up at a later point, I don't know how it's going to affect the cross-examination or my client's rights under Article 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you have brought this to the attention of Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I take it that Mr. Re will take action on the request. Yes, I see you nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that's on the record. Then on the 12th of March, the parties have mentioned an agreement on a specific forensic issue. We'd like to be informed about it, if perhaps by way of an update to agreed facts, if anything can be reported. I'm not insisting on having it now, but I just remind the parties that if we get these kind of signals of further agreement, that the Chamber is anxious to receive that information as soon as possible. Then I think we could continue. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would there be any other administrative matters today? I will probably not be in court for the last hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have been informed about that, that we can reach you if need be. Okay, that's understood. Usually if you pass these messages to Chamber staff, we'll hear from it and there's no need to repeat it in court. Only if communication goes wrong, then of course we spend a lot of time on it. Mr. Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Whilst the witness is being brought in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- there are one or two procedural matters that I intended to raise at the conclusion of this witness's evidence concerning, in particular, the order of witnesses and questions related to that. So I don't know if Mr. Re was planning to remain, but it would be helpful to have him here after Mr. Dutertre's re-examination is concluded, if only for a short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radosevic, you'll further be examined by Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. Will you allow me to make a preliminary statement regarding the explanation I provided when I talked about Dasinovac and the lake and how the bodies had been transported to Hotel Pastrik. The interpretation booths told me that there had been a change-over, and the translation of what I said from French into English did not wholly reflect what I had said, and I would like to address this again, if it is possible. Just very briefly, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only question I always have in this respect is whether it's something that should be said in the presence of the witness and the witness hearing about it, but there's no major problem here, I think. But in general terms, always the parties are invited to consider whether statements, especially if these statements are about the facts, whether it would be appropriate to do it in the presence of the witness. But here it seems to be no problem, I see from the body language of the Defence teams. Mr. Dutertre, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If necessary, the Defence counsel can interrupt as they wish. [In English] I said that the remains were found at the intersection of the roads between Dasinovac and Ratis, and these remains have been brought to canal Radonjic to be secured there. When the Serbian forensic team arrived, these remains have been handed over to them in a black plastic bag, in one. During the autopsy and identification process, Milos Radunovic and Slobodan Radosevic were identified by traditional means and their remains have been given back to the families, which means that the body of Slobodan Radosevic has been given back to the family of the witness. But from this bag some parts of bones were not matching with the rest of the bones identified. These bones, therefore, have not been given back to the families but put in a plastic bag, and this bag was put in a coffin that was buried in Piskote cemetery. In this coffin, there were other bones in other plastic bags; that means there were no co-mingling but there were several plastic bags with several bones in one coffin. In addition to what I have said, in 2003 the DNA identification process made positively that one of -- part of these bones that were in the coffins from one plastic bag were belonging to the remains of Slobodan Radosevic. So that's what I wanted to tell and that was not completely translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I've certainly no objection. I think it goes rather further in detail than simply a repetition of what was said before. I hear what Mr. Dutertre has to say as to how the Prosecution puts its position. The critical point that I was putting to this witness, I think, is not in dispute; namely, that remains were -- the remains were removed from the position where they are recorded as having been found to the Lake Radonjic canal area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Dutertre, perhaps it's time to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall address a number of issues step by step. Now, as far as the witness testimony which I gave to a non-governmental organisation, Mr. Emmerson cross-questioned you yesterday about the testimony you gave to this organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for your information, this is on page 51 and 52 and 53 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson asked you whether this organisation had made things up as pertains to what you had stated in your evidence. I would like to clarify a number of points here. First of all, could you tell us how much time elapsed between the moment when you were beaten up by KLA soldiers and the moment when you gave this testimony to the said non-governmental organisation, please?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was maybe seven or eight days, something like that. Seven or eight days after my capture, as far as I can remember. I don't know exactly, but that would be it. Seven or eight days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Secondly, we know that the police took you away so that you could receive medical treatment. Once you were released, what was your physical condition when you gave this testimony to the non-governmental organisation?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a bad state. I had been beaten up, I was under a lot of stress, and I was still very much affected by what had happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you've anticipated my next question. In other words, in what psychological state were you? And you've just answered and you've just said that you were stressed. Another question: Did you sign anything? Did you sign a document when you gave this testimony to this non-governmental organisation?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall, given the state I was in, I did not sign anything. I really can't remember. But as far as I can recall, I isn't sign anything, but I can't be sure because it's been a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Did you receive a copy of your statement provided by this NGO, or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I am now going to move on to another point, Mr. Radosevic. This relates to your -- how you were related to Zoran Nikic. I shall make it short. Mr. Emmerson asked you what degree of kinship there was between you and Zoran Nikic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was on page 58, and this was 76 to 82 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, amongst other questions he put to you, referred to the interview via videolink, an interview which it taken place between another lawyer, myself and you. And he read out the notes that had been taken thereof, and he stated: "My cousin Zoran Nikic, head of the Decani police, was told that the bodies had been located." So a very simple question I'd like to put to you: The notes that had been taken during this videolink interview, that had taken place between you, I, and Mrs. Valabhji, were these notes read back to you after the interview?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not after the conversation. They were not read back to me. But let me repeat once again: Zoran Nikic is not a member of my -- he is not a close kin. He's a -- I consider him to be a relative far passed, but he informed me about --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In the previous question you had said -- the question had been put by the NGO -- I'm going back a little bit. You said that you were stressed. How would you describe this? How stressed were you?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was under a lot of stress. I kept remembering about what had happened to me. I kept having those flashbacks. And I was very depressed and I kept thinking about what was happening with my father, so I really was depressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I shall move on to a third topic which relates to a weapon belonging to the Stijovic family. Mr. Emmerson put you questions yesterday and today on the weapon owned by the Stijovic family, and he asked you whether it was the first time you tried to get hold of the Stijovic weapon in Bandera, and you answered, if I remember correctly, "I don't remember?"

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on page 84 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: After this Q and A session with Mr. Emmerson, one had the feeling you'd never mentioned that you wanted to pick up this weapon at the Stijovic's house. Do you remember that during the proofing session we had on the 7th of March via videolink, a session between you, I, and Mrs. Valabjhi, do you remember having mentioned that you wanted to fetch the weapon that was at Novak Stijovic's father's house?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't be sure. I'm not sure about this question. I have all those things going through my mind and I can't really be sure, and I don't want to confirm anything that I'm not absolutely certain of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
