utterances.text: The question of the weapon belonging to the father --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, but I think if the matter is going to be put arising out of cross-examination, it should be accurately put. What I asked was whether or not he had told Mr. Dutertre, or indeed said in his witness statement, that he had stopped at the house of the Stijovics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you agree, would you please reformulate your question, Mr. Dutertre. We can check whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did you, when we had this videolink interview on the 7th of March, mention the fact that you tried to find Novak Stijovic's father in order to get hold of this weapon?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember discussing this issue. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: We are still discussing the same issue. Mr. Emmerson questioned you about the proofing notes of the 12th of March which had to do with the "Spotlight" document and, more specifically, to those portions of the text which related to what you had done with the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to display Exhibit 6, and turn to page 18, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 18, there is a paragraph - this was written in 1998 - which mentions what you did with these weapons and what your intentions were. Does this tally with what happened in reality?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, perhaps you could adjust the microphone for the witness. And could you speak a bit louder, Mr. Radosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I don't know what paragraph we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paragraph which is marked here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not marked anymore. It's the last paragraph above 9.2, and it's now -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it now, Your Honour. It is only true that I did not take the carbine to the KLA in Gradina but I gave it to Caus, and then I went to Decani to fetch Novak's rifle. So I didn't go back to the headquarters. I was stopped at Bandera by Caus and then we went to Pozar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, it was your weapon you had on you and not the weapon belonging to the Stijovic family, according to what is written here in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I handed over my father's carbine, not Novak's. I think there's a translation error here because it says here that I -- it says here Novak Stijovic's carbine, where, in fact, I had told them that I had wanted to go and get Novak's carbine in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: This is what it says in the English text, and this is why I elicited a comment from you about this paragraph. Mr. Radosevic, you learnt about your father's death around the 10th of September and you went on the spot the next day. What frame of mind were you in and what was your psychological state of mind when you went there?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I felt bad. Well, you can't really describe this emotional state. I did not lose a chicken; I lost my father, my next of kin. And he was only supposed to put me on my own two feet, and now he would no longer be able to do that, so it was a very difficult time for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You had this meeting with this friend of yours, this Albanian friend, who reported to you what had happened when your father and Milos Radunovic had been abducted. This was on the same day, was it?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Another point I'd like to clarify. This has to do with the identification process of their remains at the Pastrik Hotel in Djakovica. Mr. Emmerson showed you two testimonies, one which was of August 2005 and the other was December 2005. In the first, you indicated having seen the bodies; and in the second, you indicated having not been permitted to see your father's body. Do you remember having addressed this issue during the videolink proofing session on the 7th of March between you, I, and Mrs. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we did talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And what explanation did you provide?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation was that we were not allowed to see the remains of our late father, but the explanation was also that there, next to the clothes, the heap of clothes, there was something covered by a black bag, and it was apparent that these were the mortal remains. And the pathologist advised us not to try and identify the mortal remains, just the clothes that he had been wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And you identified his clothes?

utterances.speaker: STANISA RADOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to put further questions to the witness? There's one matter I'd like to raise. Mr. Radosevic, do you understand English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little, but I can't answer in English. I know a few words, just to greet somebody and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you to take your earphones off for a second. Mr. Emmerson, part of your examination was about whether this witness was ever told by his friends about another incident, a person being shot in the knee. Will this Chamber ever get a follow-up to that? Of course, the answer of the witness was clear that -- and there seems to be some case law developing, not in all systems in the world the same approach taken, on whether or not a party should -- if it comes to such specific questions, whether and when a party should lay a foundation or give further information on the basis of these rather specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Allow me to indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The position is that the Prosecution is in possession of a witness statement from the man concerned in which he describes driving to Dashinoc and being shot by this witness's father and being injured in the leg, and so forth. They're also in possession of a statement from a witness who they are proposing to call. They're not proposing at the present time to call the person concerned, but they are proposing to call a man whose name I put to this witness as a friend of his who described having heard that this witness's father shot the man concerned. And what I was putting to this witness was whether his friend, whose statement includes that he had heard that that is what had happened, had told him that that is what had happened, and we are going to hear from the witness whose statement includes the fact that he had heard that that is what had happened. Does that make the position clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least, of course, you'll understand that if the Chamber is listening to such a line of questioning, hears the answers, then, of course, the Chamber wonders whether the information might have any relevance for matters of questions of reliability, credibility, and therefore I was just wondering whether we would have any follow-up at any stage, or whether this would just be it. I do understand there will be a follow-up. I see, Mr. Dutertre, you're nodding yes as well. So the Chamber will then just wait at least until there's any ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radosevic, there was a procedural issue I wanted to discuss with the parties. That's the reason why I asked you to take off your headphones, because I did not know whether there would be any further questions for you. It now turns out that there are no further questions for you. This means that this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for having answered for quite some time questions from both parties, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you show the witness out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is one technical issue. A few lines have been read to the witness from, I think, proofing notes which were not provided with a number, although usually if something is shown to the witness, it should receive a number so that we know what has been presented to the witness. At the same time, if it's clear -- if the source is clear and if it's just one, two, or three lines read out carefully - and I checked that it was, apart from one word, that was a literal quote - then the Chamber would not insist on having it in evidence unless, of course, the Prosecution would consider that not fair under the circumstances, not even to have it on the record. I mean, what is on the record is the quote read by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think, if I may just say, all of the documents that I put to this witness have been marked for identification, apart from that one proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And Your Honour had indicated at the very outset of these proceedings that, as a general proposition, everything should be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm entirely content for that one document simply to be referred to on the transcript, but -- unless the Prosecution has any issue with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't object whatsoever to it, and I think if it's to be tendered into evidence, that this is all part of Mr. Emmerson's cross-examination. I have nothing against it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we leave it as it is for the time being. [In English] Is the Prosecution ready to -- no, Mr. Emmerson, you had some procedural issues you'd like to raise after the conclusion of the evidence of this witness. You're in a position to do so. But before that, Madam Registrar, is there any document marked for identification, which is tendered and which we would have to decide whether to admit it or not? Could you please read the documents so that we'll hear whether there's any objection. Madam Registrar, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are only Exhibits number D5 and D7 marked for identification. All the others are already admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, any objection against the admission of D5 and D7?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against D5, D7? I see you nodding "no." That's on the record. D5 and D7 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Emmerson -- I think all the P documents were -- we decided already on admission. Mr. Emmerson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if we might take stock of two issues arising in relation to witness order. The position is, as Your Honour knows, is that the next witnesses are the witnesses with the pseudonyms 19 and 4. That is on the witness list in their provisional order 27 and 29, and they obviously will be giving evidence today and tomorrow. The witness who we had some difficulty dealing with on Friday; that is to say, the witness who was number 8 on the witness list, is not to be called this week. The Prosecution will, however, call the witness who appears on Your Honours' witness list as witness number 11 who had a pseudonym of 49. Does Your Honour have that witness's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I haven't got it yet. Let me have a look. Number 11, pseudonym 49, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, the position is that, having considered that witness's statement, it contains a great deal of material which involves an expression of belief and opinion as to various aspects of the state of activity of the KLA. He is a civilian and none of the sources are identified in the witness statement. So there's a lack of transparency in the witness statement -- with one or two exceptions, there is a lack of transparency as to the sources in the statement itself. Now, I understand that he's being brought to The Hague at some point this week and obviously before he gives evidence on Friday, and I'm very anxious that we ought, at this stage, to have on the record a request that the proofing sessions with this witness clarify exactly what is known about sources of any particular statement or conclusion that the witness is purporting to give so that all parties can see, before statements are handed to the Trial Chamber and, indeed, particularly before the witness is called, what the provenance of these conclusions properly is, so that one isn't exploring these witnesses, as happened with the last witness, in the course of his testimony for the first time. It follows on from that that we would request as detailed and as near-to-verbatim as possible a record of that process. Now, I don't wish to trade over old ground, but I think there is an issue that, if I may say so, has been left hanging. With the last witness, it might not be said to be absolutely critical, although potentially whether the word used for "relative" and the word used for "cousin" are the same has some possible significance. But with the first witness where the issue came up, that is, Witness 38, it was an absolutely critical point. If Your Honours will remember, it was whether or not she had told the Prosecution during her proofing session that the jeep had arrived after she had been maltreated and stripped naked. Absolutely an crucial question, because it had never, on the face of the documents, been said either in her statement or in her proofing notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How critical it was, of course, depends on who was in the jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, of course. But in terms of understanding the reliability of the witness as a whole, which goes to that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter is clear. It's clear that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I know Your Honour was -- Your Honours were deciding how to approach the issue, but obviously the longer the trial proceeds - and we have another witness coming where very similar questions are going to arise, and it's not too late to establish how the Prosecution should approach proofing - the longer the trial occurs with the proofing process taking place without those clarifications having been made and without a record being made, the more frequently the sort of issues will arise in which potentially Prosecution counsel could be called upon to make statements which contradict their own witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a matter -- okay. The position about Prosecution counsel in this respect is still a matter for consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Nobody is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's not deal with that at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, did you -- do you intend to record, for example, if only an audio record. I know that Mr. Guy-Smith wanted to have a video record as well, but are you considering to, well, let's say, to intensify the recording of proofing sessions to the extent that it's not just short, written notes of the results, but to record them in any other way?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have no present intention to audio or video proofing sessions, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it you are aware that, sometimes more important, sometimes less important, issues arose which might have been settled relatively easily by having available an audio recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We, of course, understand, and I know the Trial Chamber understands the process, which is people are interviewed in the field by investigators, five, six, seven years- years- ago and then they're spoken to by lawyers later, and inevitably there will be differences in what people have said every time they recount a story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm not saying that. I mean perhaps even the Judges or the Chamber might be a bit -- might be a bit suspicious if never there was any inconsistency or contradiction that would raise other thoughts. But the issue is that now and then a matter comes up which is sometimes easily resolved by just having a recording there, and I just wonder whether we could not save a lot of time, really at very low expenses, to have this recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The matter is under consideration at the moment. There may be a solution, compromised solution, which doesn't go as far as Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith suggests or the present situation. We're considering that at the moment. I'll be able to report back to you, not today but very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the issue has been raised specifically in view of a witness to appear which, from what I understand in earlier statements, has not given much information; whereas, the amount of hearsay evidence, whether firsthand, secondhand, thirdhand, I don't know, seems to be considerable. So therefore to that extent the matter is relatively urgent. And, I mean, equipment in this respect might not be really causes great concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nothing will change with the witness Mr. Emmerson is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nothing will change at the moment, as of today, or what happened in terms of speaking to him in the days preceding or the years preceding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Because he's not here, and we're not planning to talk to him today. He will be here within the next -- probably tomorrow, so nothing is going to change in respect of him and what's happened before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, what I'm saying to you is, if you leave it with me, it's under consideration, and I can report back to you probably tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can't change the past, that's clear. If the witness arrives tomorrow, I think the -- Mr. Emmerson would very much like you to have at least, to start with, an audio recording of your conversations with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That if any such issue arises, that preferably not in court, because if you have a proofing session of three hours, then, of course, the Chamber is not interested to hear all of the three hours. And I take it that Mr. Emmerson will also consider how important it is before he starts listening to all these three hours. The issue simply is -- but perhaps, listening to your answer, I leave it to the two of you for the time being to see whether the day after tomorrow we have to say that, Nothing changed yesterday, or that perhaps matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just forgive me. Two very short observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The point that arose with Witness 38 is an illustration not of a difference between what somebody said seven years ago and what they said in their -- in their testimony but between what they said on Tuesday and what they said in court. The two are, in fact, in contradiction to one another. And I specifically put to her: Did you tell Mr. Di Fazio, whilst he was proofing you, what you are now telling us in evidence? And in a situation like that, it's difficult - and this is the second point - and Mr. Re says there are no current plans to change the arrangements, but so far I haven't heard him indicate why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he's also said that he's considering something.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'd like you to discuss during the break -- for you to find out what Mr. Re is considering and perhaps for Mr. Re also to give some information on what keeps him from having plans at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is one other matter, but I think Mr. Guy-Smith may have a word to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's with regard to the issue that is just at hand which is Mr. Re considering. This issue has now been live since January 19th when I wrote a letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm more than happy -- and I made a number of suggestions depending on what could work, which was video, audio, or stenographic recording. If the difficulty is a matter of cost, I'm happy to buy Mr. Re a or the OTP a tape-recorder and the appropriate number of tapes. I think we're now reaching the point where the statement that's under consideration no longer really -- really answers the question. It's been under consideration now for close -- well, over a month, and I think we need to get an answer to it because this issue most probably will arise again. Based on all of our experiences, this is not something which is new, it is not something which is unusual. And when critical information has this particular kind of a point, we need to have some verbatim understanding of what happened during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Parties are invited -- yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, unusually, I do have something to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: As my learned associate Mr. Troop points out to me, the cost in terms of all the people gathered in this room who have been spending now many or probably at least an hour today and on other days considering this issue, the cost in terms of the time that is wasted going over points which could be resolved absolutely simply outside court by providing us with videotape, audiotape, transcription, whatever it maybe. There is a cost that is out of all proportion to the problem that's being created by failing to record these matters. I just make that observation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The other matters, Your Honour, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So parties are invited to look at it. And if I may make one suggestion: Tape-recorders is old-fashioned technology, Mr. Guy-Smith. You buy for almost nothing a high quality recording device which uses memory cards, and you can keep them for a couple of days. Memory cards cost approximately $20 each, and then you use them again. They take 30 hours each of recording. Technically, it's a minor thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm an old-fashioned kind of guy, but I do appreciate the suggestion and I'll buy that for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. That deals with the position so far as this week is concerned. We were informed yesterday by Mr. Re that Colonel Crosland, who was scheduled to give evidence on Wednesday and Thursday of next week, is unable to attend, and whilst all of us, I think, would like to see his evidence as early in the trial as possible, because he's a truly independent international to that extent who was on the field -- in the field at the time, somebody who Your Honours might find an important witness, obviously from everybody's point of view we would be keen that he be available as soon after next week as is possible. At present, as I understand it, the position is that we would expect Witness number 8 on the list, that is to say, the witness about whom there was some controversy of timing, to be coming at some point next week, and probably towards the beginning of next week, and then Witness 14 on the list, whose first initial is an M, and Witness 21 on the list, a relative of that witness whose first initial is a G. We've been informed today that, in addition, Witness 23, whose first initial is a B, may also be available next week. That is the present state of our understanding, and I put it on the record lest there should be any changes in relation to it. So the two issues are that those are the witnesses that we have been informed of for next week, together potentially with any of the witnesses who answered to the subpoenas that Your Honours have issued; and secondly, that Colonel Crosland's availability -- he's one of those witnesses for whom cross-examination preparation takes, as Your Honours can imagine, some considerable time. He's given evidence in a number of cases in this Tribunal, and obviously one needs notice of when he's going to come. But also he's a witness that one wouldn't want to leave, if one had the choice, to the back-end of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, can you inform us on whether the unavailability of Mr. Crosland would result in a long delay or that he could be called relatively early in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All things are relative. The alternative dates the British Foreign and Commonwealth Office gave us were two dates when the courts wasn't sitting, the Easter break, and a later date in April; or the alternative was Monday and Tuesday next week, which just won't work. It would have to be later in April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would be the Easter break, we even could consider, but I'm just suggesting this to the parties, one of the Judges will not be available; at the same time we have, of course, a full recording. Of course, the Chamber could consider to sit with two Judges, which is not perfect, but we have to balance whether it's better to have the evidence of Mr. Crosland at an early stage and then spend one or two days during the Christmas break -- during the Easter break, or whether we would say, No, a full bench is more important and then have that delayed. The parties are invited to express themselves on the matter soon, and perhaps even some conversation amongst the Judges -- among the parties could assist the Chamber in deciding whether or not we'd sit during -- which is only a four-day week anyhow, because the second -- I don't know whether there's any specific name, but the day after Easter is a UN holiday, so that would be from Tuesday until Friday. Would the parties please consider that, what option they would prefer. Yes, for example, Wednesday or Thursday. I don't know how much time the witness is scheduled. It might be -- could someone tell me where I'd find him on the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It goes without saying that even if the parties would agree, that, of course, the Chamber itself also would have to consider whether or not this would be a solution. But I'm just -- it would be an option not to be excluded on from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He's witness number 17. Again, I don't want in any way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Scheduled for two hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say I think that may prove to have been a conservative estimate of his evidence-in-chief, and he's one of those witnesses in respect of whom we've given Your Honours notice that his cross-examination is likely to be extensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution will, of course, take Your Honours' suggestion on board yesterday which was to try and put more evidence into the form under the old 89F, which is Rule 92 ter. In our submission, or my assessment, a lot of his evidence could go into that form. The dates which the British FCO has given us, I think, are the 19th and 20th of April, which is after the Easter break. We discussed this with Defence counsel yesterday and there seemed to be no rabid objection to those particular dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you consider that. And, of course, the Chamber itself also prefers to be always complete, even though it's possible to watch a recording of the session. That's not what the Chamber prefers to do. Then, Mr. Re, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. There will be a change of Prosecution team. I understand they should be outside the court. The court is a little small to accommodate everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next witness is Witness 19, who has a pseudonym, protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Protective measures ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the protective measures include voice distortion, which needs some preparation of approximately 20 minutes, we'll have the break first and we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Witness 19, because that's how I'm going to call you, Witness 19, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 19, we are not using your name. You will testify in this court where no one will see your face out of this courtroom, no one will hear your voice - that will be distorted as well - and we'll address you by calling you Witness 19 and not use your name. Nevertheless, your testimony ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was some confusion. Nevertheless, what you tell us can be heard by the public. If there would be any answer you'd like to give in which you say, I'd rather not the outside world hear what I'm telling, if they can't see your face, they don't hear your voice because it's distorted, then please tell us. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and the text will now be handed down to you by Mr. Usher. Would you please make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 19. Please be seated. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. May we go into private session for a brief moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I want you to cast your mind back to 1998, the early part of 1998. Were there any -- did your family know in early 1998 any Serbian police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes. In 1998, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, in 1998. Was your family friends or did they know any Serbian policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: In 1998, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Slobodan Prascevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yeah, I know who he is. In 1998, we had a friendship with Slobodan. He was a Prascevic. He was a friend of my father until he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Following your father's death in the year that you told us of, did this man, this Serbian police officer, continue his friendship with your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And in early 1998, were you and your brothers and your sisters living in the small village that you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did this Serbian police officer visit in early 1998, visit your family in your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1998 did your mother -- was your mother wounded in any sort of attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When this happened, was she with this man, this Serbian police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I now want to ask you some details with that episode, okay? So focus your mind on that episode? First of all, can you tell us the date that that happened. Now, if you can't, if you can't tell us the date, can you tell us the month? If you can't tell us the month, can you tell us the season? But I want you to think back and try and give us as accurate a time for this episode, first of all, and then I'll ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: This event took place in 1998. I don't remember the date. Most probably it must have been the beginning of autumn because it was hot, but not very hot. It was an average hot weather. To my recollection, I think it may have been autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. You think it was autumn. Fine. And can you remember where you were at the time that you first became aware of any episode or incident involving this Serbian police officer and your mother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Maybe 100, 150 metres far from our house when this happened. I was at home. I was taking care of the cows. I was in the vicinity of the house with my sisters when I heard of the accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, that's a detail you remember, that you were looking after the cows and that was outside, in the open air; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Just to make things easier, don't -- when I ask you a question, don't just nod your head if you agree. Make sure you say yes or no or say something because it needs to be picked up by the microphones. So nodding your head is not enough, okay? Now, just on a side issue, during the winter in your part of the world, are cows kept inside, under shelter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: At the time of the accident, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: During winter, winter. During winter are cows kept inside, sheltered inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: No. Inside, inside. We keep them inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Does the fact that you were outside looking after cows help you with the period of time that this episode might have happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Most probably it was autumn, the beginning, early autumn when there is no snow or it's not very cold, and it was a time that the cows can find something to graze at. So I was taking care of the cows, as I said, not far from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: All right. Now, turn your mind to the actual episode itself where your mother was injured. You said you were at home looking after the cows. What did you first notice that drew your attention to the episode? What did you see or hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: I heard shots and then after a while I saw smoke coming out from that direction, but I was young and scared to go and see what had happened. I talked with my sisters, who were at home, and one of the sisters went to see what happened and she saw also smoke and she came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, on this day had the Serbian police officer that you knew, that you've mentioned already, had he come to visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did he have a car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes, he had a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour and the make of the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: The colour was red and the make was Lada. As far as I know, it was a red Lada.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, did you later ascertain that this car had been shot at and your mother was in it, and she had been injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes. We later learnt that she was wounded during this accident with the police -- policeman. We heard about this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just, unfortunately, need to go, very, very briefly, back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Was the policeman killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: We heard that he died as a result of this accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Was the brother who you've mentioned to us, who was involved in the -- was there at the scene, involved in the episode, was he okay or was he injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Fortunately, he wasn't wounded or injured. Nothing happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And finally, do you know what injuries your mother sustained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: I know that she had three or four injuries, but I cannot explain the nature of the injuries, what kind of injuries these were. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fair enough. Can you tell the Trial Chamber if they -- if she was struck by bullets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, did you eventually, after some weeks, get to see your mother in hospital and did she eventually return, after recovering, back to the family house in the small village that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes. She stayed in hospital for two or three weeks, and after she was released from hospital she returned to the village where we lived, and she lived together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just going back to the episode that we've been talking about, very briefly. Firstly, can you tell the Trial Chamber if you recall this as having happened in the morning or the afternoon -- or night, and indeed if you can give us a specific time, do? But if you can't, tell us if it happened morning, afternoon or night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Are you referring to the accident that involved my mother and this policeman?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: That's right, involving the Lada and the shooting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: It could have been afternoon, between 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your village, is there an orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes. To my knowledge, it is situated at 200 or 300 metres away from our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What's the name of the church? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: I don't remember the name, but I know that it was called the church of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, from information that -- I'll rephrase that. Can you tell the Trial Chamber where in relation to that church that this incident involving your mother and the Lada and the Serb policeman happened? Using the church as a reference point, have you got any idea where it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: It happened between the church and our house, somewhere halfway. That is where this accident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. The village in which you lived, can you tell us if there was a predominantly Albanian population living there or predominantly Serb or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: It was a mixture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: About how many Serbs lived in the village, would you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: I don't know the numbers, but there were several households. But as I said, I don't remember the exact number of these inhabitants and of the households.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thinking back, doing the best you can, how often would you say that this Serb policeman visited your family home in this village? I'm speaking about the period of time prior to the episode where your mother was wounded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: It would happen that he would visit once or twice a week. Sometimes it was once a month or twice a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he ever turn up in a police car or was it always a private car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: His own car, yes, but he used to come with another vehicle, make Niva. But mostly he came with his own private car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. And just before I leave this topic, the Niva that he came with, was that a marked police car or was is an ordinary civilian car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: It was an ordinary civilian car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. About this time that the episode happened, did you see the presence of soldiers in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: During that time or you mean later?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I mean around that time and in the ensuing weeks, in the ensuing weeks after the episode.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: When this policeman used to come with that Niva car, I didn't happen to see soldiers in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What about ensuing weeks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question very well. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Sure, no problem. In the ensuing weeks following this episode involving your mother being wounded, did you see the presence of -- did you become aware of the presence of any soldiers in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: You mean after this policeman died, that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, after the policeman died.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What sort of soldiers were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: With black clothes, with car - they would drive up and down the village and in other places - and with the KLA insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you describe the KLA insignia that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: The eagle was in the middle and the sign UCK was on the top. It was a small insignia, not very big, and it was usually worn on the arm and on the cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What colour did this have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my recollection, it was red and with black.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the witness mentioned another colour. The interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the -- you said: "Red, black," and you mentioned another colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter doesn't understand this word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A lily colour, purplish colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I just want to get a bit more data about this phenomenon that you observed. First of all, you started to see these men. You noticed them, at least, after the episode involving your mother and Serb policeman; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: They drove up and down the village streets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: After my mother died, I started to see soldiers with black clothes, with cars, with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm not talking about the period of time after your mother died. Let's go back to the period of time -- hear me out. Just listen to what I say. I'm talking about the period of time now, okay, the period of time after your mother was shot at and wounded, okay, the period of time following that, okay, and before anything happened to your sisters, okay? Now, that's the period I'm talking about. Not later but that period of time. Now, you've told us that during that period of time, or within the period of time immediately after your mother was wounded, you saw men and you've told us that they had black uniforms and you've told us about their insignia; you told us about they're driving up and down in cars. That's the period of time I'm talking about. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Okay. You are referring to the very day when my mother was wounded, to that day, or for another -- to another period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- I'm asking you about general observations you made, what you saw, of soldiers in your village. Now, you've told us that you saw soldiers after your mother was wounded; you've told us that. You've told us that you saw them in cars; you've told us that they were in black uniforms, and you've told us about the little insignia that they had on their uniform. Now, do you remember all that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: The day when my mother was wounded -- the day when my mother was wounded, I saw two or three soldiers. They were wearing black clothes. They had masks on their heads, and they were driving along the roads. This was on the day when my mother was wounded. After this day, I also saw soldiers but not immediately after the wounding of my mother. Maybe a month later. It started to become more transparent, this presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And that's exactly what I want to ask you about. You now understand what I'm asking you about. I'm asking you about how often you would see these soldiers in the period of time after your mother was wounded. How often would you say you saw them? Once a month, six times a day, once a fortnight? Try and give the Judges some idea of how often you would see them in your village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: At that time, I was more or less young. I didn't go out in the village very often. I was scared. Maybe it happened that I saw them twice a week, sometimes once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Now, when you saw them on these occasions, were they all dressed in black or were only some dressed in black? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: At all times during that time when I saw them, they were in black clothes with the KLA insignia, with weapons. After some time they had camouflage clothes, KLA camouflage clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know what sort of vehicles they would use? Just ordinary passage cars or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes; sometimes I would see them using jeeps; sometimes, ordinary cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Right. I now want to ask you if any of these men ever came to your house, your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: You're referring to the three accused or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. I'm not referring to any of the accused. I'm talking about the men that you've just been speaking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: That's okay. There's no need for apologies. Just listen to what I ask you. These men that you said you saw driving, wearing the black uniforms, who were armed, sometimes in jeeps, wearing the KLA insignia, did any such men ever come to your house, to your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: I don't remember that they came. I could not recognise their faces. They were wearing the black KLA clothes. I was scared to look at them from closer distance. I would usually look at them from a longer distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Aslan Rexhepi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Xhevat Islami?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Sokol Zefi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Were they -- did you ever see those men in these black uniforms that you've mentioned, armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them in black uniforms, armed, but sometimes they were wearing ordinary uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever see those men in the vicinity of your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. Where? How close to your home? Tell the Trial Chamber how close to your home you saw these men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Maybe 5, 10 metres away, when they came to talk, to discuss something with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Right. Okay. So you've told us that they came to your house, and they came to discuss something with your family. Now, that's what I want to talk about that, okay? You're focused on that? You understand? I'm talking about men --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: -- KLA men coming to your home, all right? That's what I'm now going to talk to you about, okay? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: All right. Tell the Trial Chamber how often -- if it happened more than once or only once, tell us? But tell us how often such visits occurred.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: First, it was two or three times a week; that is, they came during day-time. They discussed with my family. They asked for some things. Then after a while, a month or so, they came rather more often to discuss with my family, with my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, did they only ever come during the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: At the time they always came during the day-time, when they started coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And was there always more than one of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Sometimes they were in groups of four or five, sometimes in a group of three, four. More or less around this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you remember what was discussed, what they came to discuss, at your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Tell us. What was it? What was the topic of conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: They wanted weapons. They talked with my mom about this policeman, how was it that she had contacts with him and such things?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, did your family, your mother and your sisters and brothers, own any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: No. My dad, some years ago, worked and the state gave him a weapon to use. He was a forest ranger, so he had a licence to carry a weapon. After his death we surrendered his weapon, and because of that weapon they kept asking my family for more weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you know if your mother provided them any -- with any explanation as to whether or not, as to whether or not, there were any guns in your house, in your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: My mom, as far as I know, told them, We don't have any guns. We had one, But after my husband died, she said to them, I gave up the weapon because it was no good to me anymore. And she said, You can come in and search for yourselves. There is no more guns left here. But they still kept asking her for more guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did they ever search the place, your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The day they came, two or three times at the beginning they did not search. Then after that they started to search all over the house, to ransack it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And is this during day-time visits, during light?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Not during the day. It happened very rarely at day-time. Mostly it happened when they came at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you some questions about your sister, one of your older sisters, whose name starts with an S, and I don't think it's in dispute in this case that she disappeared from your family. What I want to know is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, there are two sisters with an S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm grateful for that, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the one that disappeared though later, and I only refer to that episode because I want you to think about time, okay, time, periods of time. The period of time I'm asking you about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: All right. Now, the period of time I'm asking you about is the time between your mom, your mother, being wounded, okay, and the time that this sister disappeared, okay? That period of time, those months or weeks, whatever they were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during that time, did these day-time visits occur, that period of time between your mother being wounded and this sister disappearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: All right. During that period of time between your mother being wounded and your sister S disappearing, did the visits also - also - include night-time visits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: During that period of time that I've mentioned between your mother being wounded and your sister S disappearing, did the ransackings or searchs of the house occur at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: When my mother was taken -- sorry, this sister, S, was taken, a time passed when they came to search the house and do these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if you ever had any night-time visits by these soldiers prior to your sister S disappearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes. They came.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And how did you feel when these men came into your house at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: I was frightened, but there was nothing I could do. I was too young. And, as I said, I was just scared. I could do nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want you to just provide a few more details before I leave this topic. You've told us about the uniforms that you've seen and the black -- and the insignia, the black uniforms and the insignia. Did the men who came to your house, either during the day or at night, did they ever have anything on their heads, ever wear anything on their heads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: They had masks and black uniforms with KLA insignia. They were armed. They had -- they were wearing masks over their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In that period of time, did the men who came to your house, either during the day or at night, ever give you any more details about where they originated from -- about which army or group in the army they were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: It was a special unit. They said, We are a special unit, that we are looking for weapons. They talked with my mother and sisters. I was sitting in a room with my brothers. I was young at the time, and I was sitting in that room when they were talking with my mom and sisters, these men, these soldiers, in black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. Think back and do your best to explain to the Trial Chamber why you used that expression "special unit." Think back, doing the best you can with your memory, and try and tell the Trial Chamber why you referred to them as a special unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: When they came at the time, they themselves said that, We are a special unit of the night, they said. That's why I referred to them by this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. "Special unit of the night," is that the expression that you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, do I -- can I assume that we'll go straight through to 2.15? It doesn't bother me. I'm in Your Honours' hands. I'd just like to know so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had 1.45 in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because that's when the morning sessions end and the afternoon session start at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. I apologise. I'd forgotten, if Your Honours please. That was my mistake. I've got my times wrong. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: All right. I now want you to turn your attention away from this particular topic we've been talking about, and I want you to think about your sister S, the one we call sister S, all right? In 1998, do you know how old she was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Maybe she was 23 or 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: She had been living in the village with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes, she lived with my family at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Now, during 1998, did there ever come a time when she left the family home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: She would go and visit my uncles together with the other sisters, stay there for three or four days. These were short visits. She would not stay for a week or two there. These were uncles on my mother's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'm not really talking about visits to your uncles or things like that. Did there ever come a time when she left the family home for something other than these family -- visits to relatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did she ever join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I want you to tell us about that. How did that occur, that your sister S joined the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: One night I remember when they came wearing masks, three, four, or five of them who came to our house. It was around 10.00 or 11.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to ask you some details -- some more detailed questions about this, but what I'd like you to tell the Trial Chamber first is this: Anything you tell the Trial Chamber about this episode, is it based on what you were told or what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: These were things that my mother told me, because at that time I was asleep. What we are talking about now is what my mother told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly what I wanted to know, your source of information. When did your mother tell you about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: My mother said to me -- well, that night my sister was taken, and as I said I was asleep and I couldn't see anything for myself, and she told me that her sister -- correction, that my sister was taken, because you don't have an elderly brother and the oldest in the family has to join. So she told me the next morning that my sister had been taken the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Did she provide you with any information as to who had taken her to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Think back and be as accurate as you can. The Judges want as much accuracy and detail as you can give them. What precisely were you told about who had taken your sister S?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: The following day my mother told me that it was Toger together with two others that entered the house. My mother invited them for a coffee. They had masks, but Toger had his mask on his head. She invited them, offered them coffee, and then he said to her that, It is necessary that we take, referring to my sister to join the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, for a moment, for the record, and for the record only, I would interpose an objection of hearsay and it will be a continuing objection, and I will not stand again with regard to what he was told in terms of this incident. I have a continuing objection on the grounds of hearsay, but I don't want to interrupt the flow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which suggests that we deny your objection. Yes. Put in these general terms, you're right in your assumption that the Chamber will, of course, take into consideration hearsay evidence to be not first-hand observation by the witness itself, but it's not inadmissible. So that extent, any objection to putting questions in relation to admission is rejected. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. The witness said something; I don't know what it was. It wasn't translated and it might be of importance. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll ask him. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "They brought her for a visit." There was overlapping. That's why it wasn't translated on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's fully understood that you can't translate two speakers at the same time, but I do ... Witness, we were informed that when I was speaking that you said something as "They brought her for a visit." Could you tell us who you were referring to at that moment? Who was brought for a visit? Where? By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So my statement was that that night my sister was taken, she was taken by Toger together with two other persons, and a week later Toger brought her again for a visit, my sister for a visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say "for a visit," you mean to visit your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were you present when your sister was brought for a visit? Did you see her at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did see her. I happened to be at home when Toger brought her. He was in the company of two or three other comrades. It was a jeep, a black jeep, that he parked outside. This visit was about 20 or 30 minutes long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you did know the person by the name of Toger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew his name. When he brought her for a visit, I could verify very well who Toger was, who Idriz Balaj was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we have only a couple of minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not going to get into the second visit now, if Your Honours please. I'll just wrap up a few matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: This issue of the name Toger, thinking back, when was the first time you heard of this individual Toger? And try and tell us in relation to this night when sister S was taken off to the KLA. Had you heard about the man Toger before that or was that your first acquaintance with the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: That night I heard his name very well, that it was Idriz Balaj, known as Toger, so I verified for myself who that person was behind that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: How did you do that? How did you verify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Verifying in a sense that a person who spoke with my mother that night when he took away my sister, he said to her, I am Toger. And to my knowledge, his name is Idriz Balaj, but at that time he was known as Toger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: And just finally one last question, if I may, before we break. What I want to know is this, tell the Trial Chamber this: Did your mother inform you that the person who had come the night before bore that name? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/19
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is this an appropriate moment, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, it is. Witness 19, we'll conclude for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning when you'll continue your testimony. I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, the testimony that you've given today but also testimony still to be given tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Everything is in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 p.m.
